newsitem.title: LEBANON: Voting begins in final round of Lebanon elections.
newsitem.headline: Voting begins in final round of Lebanon elections.

text.p: Lebanon's eastern Bekaa valley voted on Sunday in the final round of elections that could further reduce the pro-Iranian Hizbollah's strength in parliament.

Some 410,000 voters were eligible to cast their ballots in the vote for the last 23 deputies to the 128-member parliament. Only a trickle of voters turned out as the polling stations opened at 7:00 a.m. (0400 GMT) for the fifth round of regional elections that began on September 18.
A pro-government list with six ministers, several deputies and candidates of Hizbollah and the secular Amal, Lebanon's two main rival Shi'ite Moslem movements, was expected to win most of the seats..
Thew predominantly Shi'ite region is a stronghold of Hizbollah (Party of God), but the group has only three members and two supporters on the pro-government list.
If they win, Hizbollah will have a total of seven deputies and two allies in the new parliament compared with eight deputies and four allies now.
But Hizbollah sources said they feared that some of the Bekaa's 123,000 Christian voters might delete its candidates when voting for the main ticket.
They said Christians were angered that under a Syrian-brokered deal forming the pro-government list the Maronite Christian candidate for the Baalbek-Hermel district was chosen by Hizbollah.

"The leadership of Hizbollah has called on its supporters to vote massively as a preventive method in case Christian voters boycott Hizbollah candidates," a local Hizbollah official who asked not to be identified told Reuters.

Political sources in the Bekaa said Syria, which has 35,000 troops in Lebanon, greatly influenced the composition of the pro-government list which is a disparate group of political rivals, all viewed however as allies of Syria.
Hizbollah's guerrillas, who are fighting to oust Israeli troops from a south Lebanon border strip, are an important card in Syria's hand in peace moves with Israel.

But Damascus has used the elections to show Hizbollah the limits of its independence, helping to engineer the losses it and other Moslem fundamentalist groups suffered in north and central Lebanon and then forcing it into a reluctant alliance with Amal in south Lebanon and the Bekaa, the surces said.

The opposition candidate most likely to win in the Bekka was Tarek Habchi, a Maronite representing Baalbek-Hermel on the leftist list, newspapers said. Habchi, a popular figure in the region, is a nephew of President Elias Hrawi.
But communist party secretary-general Farouk Dahrouje could also win if there was a large oppositon vote, analysts said.
